answers.why: Israel is pictured as a vine whose prosperity increases the people's altars and images.
Ephraim receives shame when Samaria's calf is carried to Assyria.
Israel's shame concerns the nation's counsel and its idol's removal to Assyria.
Israel's sinful high places and their altars are destroyed, and the people cry for cover.
Israel is addressed as having sinned since Gibeah, with plural references to those facing battle.
Ephraim is portrayed as a trained heifer in a passage about chastising the people.
Ephraim's coming labor parallels Judah's plowing in a collective agricultural metaphor.
Judah shall plow alongside Ephraim and Jacob in a metaphor addressed to the peoples.
Israel's childhood represents the nation called out of Egypt, whose people then sacrificed to Baalim.
Ephraim is described with plural pronouns as those God carried and healed.
Ephraim is God's backsliding people whom he hesitates to destroy like Admah.
Israel parallels Ephraim as the people threatened with destruction like Admah and Zeboim.
God promises to spare Ephraim, whose people will walk after the LORD.
Ephraim's lies parallel the deceit of the house of Israel.
The phrase 'house of Israel' identifies the collective people accused of deceit.
Judah is compared with Ephraim and the house of Israel in their relationship with God.
